'Sixty-two replies,' Jagdish said, scrolling. 'On the fresher post. Everyone wrote something different.'

Avni pulled the laptop closer. 'Bus timings. Library cards. Mess timings. The wifi password.'

'Wait,' said Jagdish. 'Read the ones I highlighted.'

'"Didn't know the gate closes at ten." "Nobody told me visitors aren't allowed." "Confused about laundry days."'

'All hostel rules,' said Jagdish. 'Fourteen of the sixty-two, more than any other topic. When the same thing turns up again and again from different people, it's not luck.'

'So orientation needs a hostel rules session?'

'Or one page. But first we check with the warden that these rules are the current ones.'

passage: I still remember the night we read those replies. I'm Santosh, and in second year I ran the welcome committee. We posted a simple question on the college forum: "Seniors, what confused you most in your first week?" More than eighty people answered. Madhav and I sat in the canteen with the list. At first it was just noise: Wi-Fi, mess timings, lost ID cards. Then I started tallying. I said to Madhav, "Wait. Curfew, guest rules, laundry days, getting a late pass. These are all the same thing. It's hostel rules." We counted: thirty-one replies were about hostel rules. Nobody had said "hostel rules" in those words; they were hiding in different complaints. So that year our orientation opened with a hostel-rules session, not the campus tour.

qa.a: Thirty-one replies were about hostel rules.

qa.q: How did Santosh feel when the pattern appeared?
qa.a: Santosh felt a jolt of excitement and surprise, seeing that curfew, guest rules, laundry days and late passes were all one problem.

qa.q: What would you change first if you were running the next orientation?
qa.a: Check with this year's freshers after the hostel-rules session whether it helped, and post the question again to spot any new pattern.

qa.q: How might the freshers experience orientation after this change?
qa.a: Freshers would feel less lost in their first week, since their biggest confusion is answered on day one.

Faculty adviser's note: Student Welfare Club, September

Sudha and Vandana asked for my time today to show what they found. The club had asked the online student community one question: what problems did you face in orientation? They got about sixty answers. Sudha had printed them and highlighted by colour. She explained her thinking aloud: "At first I sorted by topic and got twelve piles. Then I noticed the same worry under different names: nobody knew when the hostel gates close, whether visitors are allowed, who to ask for a late entry. That's one confusion, not twelve." Vandana added that the replies came from four different hostels. I suggested they meet the chief warden this week. They left with an appointment.

qa.q: How many answers did the club get?
What does Sudha's explanation suggest about how she felt once she spotted the pattern?
qa.a: She seems confident and relieved: twelve confusing piles turned into one clear problem about hostel rules.

qa.q: What could Sudha and Vandana do next, besides meeting the chief warden?
qa.a: They could draft a one-page hostel rules guide for freshers and share it back with the community to check it answers the confusion.

qa.q: How might the chief warden see the students' findings?
qa.a: The warden may feel informed and willing to act, since the evidence comes from four hostels, not one complaint.

grounding: A student club gathers replies from the wider community and reasons aloud about the repeated confusion around hostel rules.
